title: 1. External Sorting and Tournament Trees
content:
In this lecture, we’re going to explore how to handle sorting and organizing data when it’s too large to fit into a computer’s main memory, which is a common problem in real-world applications. When you have a huge amount of data stored on a disk, you can’t just load it all into memory, sort it, and write it back because the data size exceeds what your RAM can hold. This is where external sorting comes in. External sorting is about designing methods that minimize the slow disk operations, like reading and writing, because accessing data on a disk is much slower than accessing it in memory. The main goal is to reduce the number of times you have to move the disk’s read/write head and wait for the disk to spin to the right position.

To understand external sorting, it helps to first recall how internal sorting algorithms like quick sort and merge sort work. Quick sort is fast on average because it picks a pivot element and partitions the data into smaller groups around that pivot, then sorts those groups recursively. Merge sort, on the other hand, splits the data into smaller pieces, sorts those pieces, and then merges them back together in order. Merge sort is especially useful for external sorting because it has a predictable worst-case performance and works well with sequential data access, which is better for disks.

When adapting quick sort for external sorting, the idea is to use buffers to hold parts of the data temporarily. You have an input buffer that reads data from the disk, and then you separate the data into three groups: smaller than the pivot, equal to the pivot, and larger than the pivot. These groups are stored in separate buffers. When a buffer fills up, it’s written back to disk. This buffering helps reduce the number of slow disk operations. To manage the middle group efficiently, a special data structure called a double-ended priority queue is used, which allows quick access to both the smallest and largest elements in that group.

External merge sort works in two main phases. First, you generate sorted runs by reading as much data as fits into memory, sorting it internally, and writing it back to disk as a sorted segment. Then, in the merging phase, you repeatedly merge pairs of these sorted runs until only one sorted run remains. This merging is done by reading blocks from two runs into memory, merging them, and writing the merged output back to disk. The number of merge passes depends on how many initial runs you have and how many runs you merge at once. Increasing the number of runs merged in each pass can reduce the total number of passes, but it also means you need more memory for input buffers, which can affect performance.

To efficiently merge multiple sorted runs, tournament trees are used. A tournament tree is a complete binary tree where each leaf represents a data element, and each internal node represents a match between two elements, storing the winner of that match. The root of the tree holds the overall winner, which is the smallest or largest element depending on the type of tournament tree. When you remove the winner, you replace it with the next element from the same run and replay the matches along the path to the root to find the new winner. This process takes time proportional to the height of the tree, which is logarithmic in the number of runs, making it efficient for merging.

There are two main types of tournament trees: winner trees, where internal nodes store the winners of matches, and loser trees, where internal nodes store the losers. Loser trees can simplify the update process when replacing the winner. Tournament trees are not only useful for merging runs in external sorting but also have applications in other problems like truck loading and bin packing.

Truck loading and bin packing are practical problems where you want to pack items of different sizes into containers or bins with fixed capacity, minimizing the number of bins used. This problem is known to be computationally hard, so exact solutions are often impractical for large inputs. Instead, heuristics are used. For example, the first fit heuristic places each item into the first bin where it fits, creating a new bin only if necessary. The first fit decreasing heuristic sorts items by size before applying first fit, which usually gives better results. Similarly, best fit places each item into the bin that will have the least leftover space after adding the item, and best fit decreasing sorts items first before applying best fit. These heuristics have known performance bounds, meaning they won’t be too far from the optimal solution.

Tournament trees can also help in bin packing by efficiently keeping track of bins and their available space, allowing quick decisions about where to place the next item. Overall, the combination of external sorting techniques and tournament trees provides powerful tools for managing and processing large data sets that don’t fit into memory, as well as solving related optimization problems.

title: 2. Run Generation, Optimal Merging, and Huffman Trees
content:
When working with large amounts of data that don’t fit into memory, sorting has to be done in stages, often involving reading and writing data to disk. One important step in this process is called run generation, where the data is broken into sorted chunks called runs. The goal here is to create as few runs as possible, and to make each run as long as possible, because fewer and longer runs make the next step—merging—more efficient. To improve run generation, it helps to overlap the work of reading data from disk, processing it in memory, and writing the sorted runs back to disk. This way, the CPU isn’t waiting for disk operations to finish, and the system runs more smoothly.

A practical way to do this is by using multiple buffers—two for input and two for output—while the rest of the memory is used to maintain a data structure called a loser tree. A loser tree is a kind of tournament tree that helps quickly find the smallest element among several sorted sequences, which is useful when merging runs. If you have k runs, the loser tree helps ensure that each run generated is at least size k, and on average, runs tend to be about twice that size. If the input data is already sorted, you only get one run, but if it’s sorted in reverse, you might get many more. The internal processing time for this approach grows in a way that’s proportional to the number of elements times the logarithm of the number of runs, which is efficient for large data.

Once you have these runs, the next step is merging them into a fully sorted sequence. But runs can be different lengths, and merging them in the right order can save time. To understand this, we use a concept called weighted external path length, or WEPL. Think of it as a way to measure the total cost of merging runs, where each run’s size is its weight, and the cost depends on how far it is from the root in a merging tree. The goal is to arrange the merging so that the total cost is as low as possible. For example, if all runs are at the same depth in the tree, the cost might be higher than if some runs are closer to the root, reducing the overall effort.

This idea of weighted cost also applies to message coding and decoding, especially in lossless data compression. Imagine you have a fixed set of messages, each with a known frequency of occurrence. Both the sender and receiver know these messages and their codes, so instead of sending the full message, you just send a code that identifies it. The challenge is to assign codes so that the total time or cost to transmit and decode messages is minimized. This is similar to minimizing WEPL, where the code length corresponds to the distance from the root in a decoding tree.

Using fixed-length codes for messages is simple but often inefficient, especially when some messages occur much more frequently than others. Variable-length codes, where more frequent messages get shorter codes and less frequent ones get longer codes, can reduce the total size of the encoded data. To make sure decoding is unambiguous, these codes must satisfy the prefix property, meaning no code is a prefix of another. This ensures that when you read a sequence of bits, you can always tell where one code ends and the next begins.

Huffman trees are a way to build these optimal prefix codes. They are binary trees constructed using a greedy algorithm that repeatedly combines the two least frequent messages into a new node until only one tree remains. This process guarantees the minimum weighted external path length, which means the codes derived from this tree are as efficient as possible. To do this efficiently, a min-heap data structure is often used to quickly find and combine the smallest weights. The whole process runs in time proportional to the number of messages times the logarithm of that number, which is practical even for large sets.

Sometimes, instead of binary trees, you might want to use trees with more than two children per node, called k-ary trees. However, the greedy method that works for binary trees doesn’t always produce the best result for these higher-order trees. The problem is that not all nodes end up with exactly k children, which can increase the total cost. To fix this, you add dummy runs with zero weight to make sure the number of runs fits the structure of a k-ary tree. This adjustment ensures that all internal nodes have the right number of children and that the merging cost is minimized.

When merging multiple runs, memory management is important. You need exactly two output buffers to allow writing to disk without waiting, and at least k+1 input buffers for the loser tree if you’re merging k runs. Sometimes, you might have 2k input buffers available, but that’s not always enough if you allocate two buffers per run. Instead, input buffers are assigned dynamically based on which run is expected to finish first. This is determined by looking at the last key read from each run and choosing the run with the smallest last key to receive the next buffer.

To start merging k runs, you initialize queues of input buffers, one per run, and load one buffer from each. Any extra buffers go into a free pool. You then begin reading the next buffer from the run that will exhaust first, using a free buffer for this. The merging process continues by moving data from input buffers to the active output buffer until the output buffer is full or an end-of-run key is reached. If an input buffer empties, you move to the next buffer in its queue and free the empty one. This cycle repeats until all runs are merged.

In summary, run generation and merging are key steps in external sorting, and using structures like loser trees and Huffman trees helps make these steps efficient. Understanding how to minimize weighted costs in merging and coding leads to better performance in sorting and compression tasks. Proper memory and buffer management during merging also play a crucial role in keeping the process smooth and fast.

title: 3. Double-Ended Priority Queues and Interval Heaps
content:
Today, we’re going to talk about double-ended priority queues and a special data structure called interval heaps. These structures are useful when you want to efficiently access and remove both the smallest and largest elements from a collection, something that regular priority queues don’t handle well because they only focus on one end—either the minimum or the maximum.

A double-ended priority queue supports three main operations: inserting a new element, removing the minimum element, and removing the maximum element. The challenge is to do all of these efficiently. One straightforward way to build such a structure is to use two separate priority queues: one min-heap for the smallest elements and one max-heap for the largest. Each element is stored in both heaps, and the two copies are linked so that when you remove an element from one heap, you can quickly find and remove it from the other. This approach works but has some downsides. It roughly doubles the space needed because every element is stored twice, and the operations become more expensive since you have to maintain two heaps and keep them synchronized.

Another approach is to split the elements between two heaps, one min and one max, but not duplicate all elements. You keep about half the elements in the min-heap and the other half in the max-heap, with a buffer for an odd number of elements. You then establish a correspondence between elements in the two heaps, pairing each element in the min-heap with a larger or equal element in the max-heap. This reduces space but requires careful management to keep the correspondence intact during insertions and removals.

Now, interval heaps offer a more elegant and efficient solution. Imagine a complete binary tree where each node holds two elements instead of one. These two elements form an interval, with the smaller element on the left and the larger on the right. The key property is that the interval of any child node is contained within the interval of its parent. This means the smallest elements are always on the left side of the tree, forming a min-heap, and the largest elements are on the right side, forming a max-heap. Because of this, the root node always contains both the minimum and maximum elements, making access to both ends very fast.

When inserting into an interval heap, the new element becomes either a left or right endpoint of an interval, depending on its value. If it’s smaller, it goes into the min-heap side; if larger, into the max-heap side. Sometimes, if the heap is empty or the new element fits perfectly, it can form an interval by itself. The insertion process involves moving the element up the tree to maintain the heap properties on both sides.

Removing the minimum element from an interval heap is a bit more involved than in a simple heap. If there’s only one element, removal is straightforward. But with more elements, you remove the left endpoint from the root, then take the left endpoint from the last node and reinsert it starting at the root to restore the heap property. If the last node becomes empty after this, it’s removed. Sometimes you need to swap elements within a node to keep the intervals valid. This process ensures the structure remains balanced and the min and max heaps are maintained.

Building or rebalancing an interval heap involves checking nodes from the bottom up. If the two elements in a node are out of order, they’re swapped. Then the right endpoint is reinserted into the max-heap and the left endpoint into the min-heap. This bottom-up approach efficiently restores the heap properties.

Performance-wise, modern processors have caches that affect how fast these operations run. Since heaps involve moving elements up and down levels, cache misses can slow things down. To improve this, we can use d-ary heaps, where each node has more than two children—say four instead of two. This reduces the height of the heap, so fewer levels need to be traversed during operations. Although each level requires more comparisons, the overall effect is often faster. Aligning the heap nodes with cache lines also helps reduce cache misses, making operations more efficient.

Interval heaps are especially useful in applications where you need to manage ranges or intervals dynamically. For example, if you have a collection of numbers and want to quickly insert or remove points, or report all points outside a certain range, interval heaps can handle these tasks efficiently. Insertions and removals take logarithmic time, and reporting points outside a range can be done in time proportional to the number of points reported.

In summary, double-ended priority queues let you work with both ends of a priority set efficiently, and interval heaps provide a neat, space-efficient way to implement them. They combine the properties of min and max heaps in a single structure, allowing quick access to both minimum and maximum elements, while supporting fast insertions and removals. Understanding these structures and their performance considerations can be very helpful when dealing with problems that require flexible priority management or range queries.

title: 4. Leftist Trees
content:
Today, we’re going to talk about leftist trees, a type of binary tree used to implement priority queues efficiently. You can think of leftist trees as a variation of heaps, but with a special structure that makes merging two priority queues much faster. Like heaps, leftist trees support the usual operations: inserting elements, removing the minimum (or maximum), and initializing the structure. What sets them apart is their ability to meld, or merge, two priority queues in logarithmic time, which is not as straightforward with regular heaps.

To understand leftist trees, we first need to look at something called extended binary trees. Imagine you have a regular binary tree, but wherever there’s a missing child, you add a special kind of node called an external node. These external nodes mark the ends of paths in the tree. If your original tree has a certain number of internal nodes, the extended version will have one more external node than internal nodes. This setup helps us define a function, called s, which measures how close a node is to an external node. For any node, s is the length of the shortest path from that node down to an external node in its subtree. If the node itself is external, s is zero. Otherwise, s is one plus the smaller s value of its two children.

Now, a leftist tree is a binary tree that follows a simple rule: for every internal node, the s value of its left child is always at least as big as the s value of its right child. This means the tree is “left-heavy” in terms of this shortest path measure. Because of this, the rightmost path from the root to an external node is always the shortest path in the tree. This rightmost path is important because it’s guaranteed to be short—specifically, its length grows logarithmically with the number of nodes in the tree. This property keeps operations efficient.

Leftist trees can be used as priority queues, either as min-priority queues where the smallest element is at the root, or max-priority queues where the largest element is at the root. The main operations you’ll use are inserting a new element, removing the minimum element, melding two trees, and initializing the tree from a collection of elements.

The meld operation is the key to leftist trees. When you meld two trees, you compare their roots and pick the one with the smaller root to be the new root. Then, you recursively meld the right subtree of this root with the other tree. After melding, you check the s values of the children and swap them if necessary to maintain the leftist property. Because the rightmost path is short, this process only touches a small part of the tree, making meld run in logarithmic time.

Insertion is done by creating a new single-node tree with the element you want to add and then melding it with the existing tree. Removing the minimum element means removing the root and melding its left and right subtrees. Both operations rely on meld and therefore run efficiently.

If you want to build a leftist tree from many elements, you can start by creating single-node trees for each element and putting them in a queue. Then, repeatedly remove two trees from the queue, meld them, and put the result back until only one tree remains. This approach builds the tree in linear time, similar to how heaps can be built efficiently.

Leftist trees also support removing an arbitrary element if you have a pointer to it. If the element is the root, it’s just a remove-min operation. If it’s not the root, you replace the node with its left subtree, adjust the s values and leftist property on the path up to the root, and then meld the right subtree back in. This operation is a bit more involved but still efficient because the tree’s height is logarithmic.

In summary, leftist trees are a useful data structure for priority queues, especially when you need to merge queues quickly. Their special leftist property keeps the rightmost path short, which makes melding and other operations fast. They support all the usual priority queue operations with good performance and can be built efficiently from a set of elements. This makes them a practical choice when merging heaps is a common operation.

title: 5. Amortized Complexity
content:
When we analyze algorithms, we often want to understand how long they take or how much work they do. There are a few common ways to measure this. One is the worst-case complexity, which tells us the maximum time an algorithm might take for any input of a given size. This is useful because it guarantees an upper limit on the running time. Another way is average complexity, which looks at the expected time over all possible inputs, giving a sense of typical performance. But sometimes, neither of these fully captures what’s going on, especially when some operations are cheap and others are expensive but rare. That’s where amortized complexity comes in.

Amortized complexity looks at the average cost per operation over a sequence of operations, rather than focusing on each operation individually. The idea is that while some tasks might be costly, they happen infrequently enough that when you spread their cost over many cheap tasks, the average cost per task remains low. This is different from average complexity because amortized analysis doesn’t rely on probability or input distribution; it’s a worst-case guarantee over sequences of operations.

To make this clearer, think about sorting with Quick Sort. In the worst case, sorting n numbers might take time proportional to n squared, which is quite slow. But on average, Quick Sort runs much faster, roughly proportional to n times the logarithm of n. The worst-case time tells us the longest it could ever take, while the average time tells us what to expect if we consider all possible inputs. However, if you only look at a few inputs, you can’t reliably say the time will be close to the average; it might be closer to the worst case. Amortized complexity helps in situations where you have a sequence of tasks, each with varying costs, and you want a meaningful upper bound on the total cost.

Imagine you have a sequence of tasks, each with some cost. The worst-case cost of any single task is some fixed number, so the total cost for all tasks is at most the number of tasks times that worst-case cost. But this can be a very loose upper bound because not every task will cost that much. The average cost per task in the sequence is the total cost divided by the number of tasks, but this average doesn’t guarantee that the first few tasks won’t be expensive. Amortized complexity gives us a better way to bound the total cost by assigning an amortized cost to each task. This amortized cost might be higher or lower than the actual cost of that task, but over the whole sequence, the sum of amortized costs will always be at least the sum of actual costs.

One way to think about amortized complexity is as a charging scheme. You “charge” each task a certain amount, which might be more than it actually costs sometimes, and less at other times. The key is that the total charged amount covers the total actual cost. This approach smooths out the spikes in cost from expensive operations by spreading their cost over many cheaper ones.

To analyze amortized complexity, we often use something called a potential function. This function keeps track of how much extra “credit” or “debt” we have accumulated as we perform tasks. After each task, the potential changes depending on how the amortized cost compares to the actual cost. If the potential is positive, it means we have overcharged so far and have some credit stored up. If it’s zero or positive at the end, it means the total amortized cost is a valid upper bound on the total actual cost.

Let’s look at a practical example involving parsing arithmetic statements. Suppose you want to rewrite an expression without parentheses using a stack and a method that processes one symbol at a time. Each time you see a symbol, you either push it onto the stack or pop symbols off the stack to form an assignment statement. Some symbols cause many pops, which might seem expensive. If you analyze the worst-case cost per symbol, it might look like the total cost is quadratic in the number of symbols. But if you look at the total number of push and pop operations over the entire sequence, it turns out to be linear. Using amortized analysis, you find that the average cost per symbol is constant, which is a much better and more realistic bound.

There are three main methods to find amortized costs. The aggregate method sums up the total cost of all operations and divides by the number of operations to get an average. The accounting method assigns an amortized cost to each operation and uses a system of credits to pay for expensive operations later. The potential function method defines a potential that measures stored credit and uses it to calculate amortized costs precisely.

Another classic example is the binary counter. Imagine an n-bit counter that starts at zero and increments by one repeatedly. Each increment flips some bits from 0 to 1 or from 1 to 0. The cost of an increment is the number of bits that change. The worst-case cost of one increment is n, when all bits flip. So, if you do m increments, the worst-case total cost could be m times n. But if you analyze it carefully, each bit flips from 0 to 1 and back to 0 multiple times, but the total number of flips across all bits and increments is less than twice m. This means the average cost per increment is constant, not linear in n.

Using the accounting method, you can think of each increment as paying two units of cost: one to flip a bit from 0 to 1 and one stored as credit to pay for flipping it back from 1 to 0 later. This credit system ensures that no operation is undercharged. The potential function method defines the potential as the number of 1s in the counter after each increment. The change in potential plus the actual cost gives the amortized cost, which again turns out to be constant per increment.

In summary, amortized complexity is a powerful way to analyze sequences of operations where some are expensive but rare. It gives a more realistic upper bound on the average cost per operation over time, without relying on probability. By using tools like the aggregate method, accounting method, and potential functions, we can rigorously prove these bounds and better understand the true efficiency of algorithms and data structures.

title: 6. Binomial Heaps
content:
Binomial heaps are a type of data structure used to manage collections of elements where you often need to quickly find and remove the smallest item, insert new items, or merge two collections together. They are especially useful when merging heaps is a common operation, something that simpler heaps like binary heaps don’t handle efficiently. At their core, binomial heaps are made up of several binomial trees, which are special trees with a very particular structure and size pattern.

Each binomial tree has a degree, which is just the number of children its root node has. These trees are linked together in a circular linked list at the top level, and each tree in the heap follows the min-heap property, meaning the root of each tree is the smallest element in that tree. The heap keeps track of the minimum element by maintaining a pointer to the root with the smallest value among all the trees.

The nodes in these trees have a few important pointers: one to a child, one to a sibling, and a degree value. The child pointer points to one of the node’s children, or is null if there are none. The sibling pointer links nodes that share the same parent, forming a circular list of siblings. This structure allows us to efficiently traverse and manipulate the trees.

When you insert a new element into a binomial heap, you start by creating a new binomial heap that contains just a single node. Then, you merge this tiny heap with the existing heap. This merging process is called melding, and it involves combining the two circular linked lists of binomial trees from both heaps. After melding, you update the pointer to the minimum element if the new node is smaller than the current minimum.

Melding is a key operation because it allows two heaps to be combined efficiently. The process involves merging the two lists of trees by their degree, making sure that there is at most one tree of any degree in the resulting heap. If two trees have the same degree, they are combined into a single tree of the next higher degree by making the tree with the larger root a child of the other.

Removing the minimum element is a bit more involved. First, you find the binomial tree whose root contains the minimum element and remove that tree from the heap. The children of this removed tree form a new set of binomial trees, which you then merge back into the remaining heap. After reinserting these subtrees, you update the pointer to the minimum element by scanning the roots of all the trees in the heap.

At first glance, this remove-min operation might seem expensive because it involves scanning and merging multiple trees, which can take time proportional to the number of elements. However, there is a way to make it more efficient by using a technique called pairwise combining. During reinsertion, whenever you find two trees with the same degree, you combine them immediately, just like in the melding process. This reduces the number of trees you have to deal with and keeps the heap balanced.

To keep track of which trees have been combined, you use a table indexed by degree. As you go through the trees, you place each one in the table according to its degree. If the table already has a tree of that degree, you combine the two and try to place the new tree back into the table. This continues until no two trees share the same degree. The remaining trees are then linked together to form the new heap.

The beauty of this approach is that the maximum degree of any tree in the heap grows logarithmically with the number of elements. This means the remove-min operation, with pairwise combining, runs in logarithmic time, which is much more efficient than the naive approach.

Binomial trees themselves are built recursively. A tree of degree zero is just a single node. A tree of degree k is formed by linking two trees of degree k-1, making one the child of the other. This recursive structure means that a binomial tree of degree k has exactly 2 to the power of k nodes. Because the heap is made up of binomial trees with unique degrees, the number of trees in the heap is at most logarithmic in the number of elements, which keeps operations efficient.

In summary, binomial heaps provide a way to manage priority queues with good performance on insertion, removal of the minimum element, and especially merging heaps. Their structure of binomial trees and the use of pairwise combining during removal help maintain balance and efficiency. Understanding how these trees are linked and combined is key to grasping how binomial heaps work and why they are useful in certain applications.

title: 7. Fibonacci Heaps and Pairing Heaps
content:
Today, we’re going to talk about two important types of heaps: Fibonacci heaps and pairing heaps. These are special data structures used to manage priority queues efficiently, especially in algorithms like Dijkstra’s shortest path. Understanding these heaps helps us improve the speed of certain graph algorithms by making operations like inserting elements, removing the smallest or largest element, and updating keys faster.

Let’s start with Fibonacci heaps. A Fibonacci heap is a collection of trees that follow the heap property, meaning the key at a parent node is always smaller (or larger, depending on whether it’s a min-heap or max-heap) than the keys of its children. What makes Fibonacci heaps interesting is how they organize these trees and how they handle operations. Instead of keeping a single tree, they maintain a forest of trees linked together in a circular doubly linked list. This setup allows some operations to be very fast on average, even if they might seem complicated at first glance.

The key operations in a Fibonacci heap include inserting a new element, removing the minimum element, melding two heaps together, and decreasing the key of a node. Insertion is straightforward and very fast because you just add a new single-node tree to the root list. Removing the minimum element is more involved because it requires consolidating trees to maintain the heap’s structure, but it still runs efficiently on average. Decreasing a key is particularly important in graph algorithms like Dijkstra’s because it happens frequently when we find shorter paths. Fibonacci heaps handle this operation very efficiently by cutting nodes from their current position and moving them to the root list if necessary, which keeps the trees shallow and balanced.

Each node in a Fibonacci heap stores several pieces of information: its degree (how many children it has), pointers to its parent and children, and a flag called ChildCut. This flag helps the heap keep track of whether a node has lost a child since it became a child of its current parent. This is important for the cascading cut operation, which is a process that helps maintain the heap’s efficiency by cutting nodes that have lost children and moving them to the root list. This cascading cut can continue up the tree until it reaches a node that hasn’t lost a child before, ensuring the heap remains balanced.

Now, let’s move on to pairing heaps, which are a simpler alternative to Fibonacci heaps. Pairing heaps also maintain a heap-ordered tree, but their structure is less complex. Each node has a pointer to its first child and pointers to its siblings, but unlike Fibonacci heaps, they don’t keep track of parent pointers, degrees, or child-cut flags. This simplicity makes pairing heaps easier to implement and often faster in practice, even though their theoretical worst-case performance isn’t as good as Fibonacci heaps.

The main operations in pairing heaps are similar: inserting a new element, removing the minimum or maximum element, melding two heaps, and decreasing or increasing keys. Insertion is done by creating a new single-node heap and melding it with the existing heap, which is very fast. Removing the minimum or maximum element involves removing the root and then melding all its subtrees back into a single heap. How you meld these subtrees matters a lot for performance. A naive approach that melds them one by one can be slow, but better methods like the two-pass or multipass schemes meld the subtrees in pairs or using a queue to keep the operation efficient.

When it comes to increasing or decreasing keys in pairing heaps, since nodes don’t have parent pointers, you can’t easily check if the heap property is violated. Instead, you detach the node from its current position and meld it back into the heap, which keeps things simple and efficient.

In summary, Fibonacci heaps offer excellent theoretical performance, especially for decrease-key operations, which makes them valuable in certain graph algorithms. Pairing heaps, while theoretically not as strong, are simpler and often faster in real-world use because they have less overhead and are easier to implement. Both heaps rely on clever ways of linking and restructuring trees to keep operations efficient, and understanding these methods helps us appreciate how data structures can impact algorithm performance.

title: 8. Dictionaries and Indexed Search Trees
content:
A dictionary in computer science is a way to store pairs of data, where each pair has a key and an element. The key is like a unique label that helps you find the element quickly. For example, you might have a dictionary of student records where the key is the student’s name and the element is their list of scores. Usually, keys are unique, so you don’t have two students with the exact same name in the dictionary. But sometimes, dictionaries allow duplicate keys, like in a word dictionary where the same word can have multiple meanings. In that case, the dictionary stores several pairs with the same key but different elements.

When working with dictionaries, there are two main types: static and dynamic. A static dictionary is created once and doesn’t change. You can search for keys, but you don’t add or remove items after it’s built. This is useful for things like a CD-ROM dictionary or a geographic database where the data is fixed. A dynamic dictionary, on the other hand, lets you search, insert new pairs, and remove existing ones. This flexibility is important for applications where the data changes over time.

One common way to implement dictionaries is with hash tables. Hash tables are popular because they can find, add, or remove items very quickly on average, usually in constant time. However, in the worst case, when many keys collide, these operations can slow down significantly. Also, hash tables aren’t good if you want to do more complex queries, like finding the closest key greater than a given one, or retrieving the third smallest key. For those tasks, other data structures are better.

A related problem is bin packing, where you have items of different sizes and bins with a fixed capacity, and you want to pack all items using as few bins as possible. One simple method is the Best Fit heuristic. You take items one by one and try to put each into the bin that will have the least leftover space after adding the item, as long as it fits. If no bin can hold the item, you start a new bin. This approach is easy to implement using a dynamic dictionary that keeps track of bins by their available capacity. Each time you add an item, you update the capacity of the bin it goes into.

Indexed binary search trees are a special kind of binary search tree that store extra information to help with operations based on the position of elements. Each node keeps track of how many nodes are in its left subtree. This allows you to quickly find the element at a certain index, like the third smallest element, without having to traverse the whole tree. You can also remove elements by their position efficiently. This is useful when you want to treat the tree like a list but still have fast search and update times.

When comparing different ways to store lists or dictionaries, arrays are fast for accessing elements by index but slow for inserting or deleting items in the middle. Linked lists are slow for access but easier for insertions and deletions. Indexed balanced trees, like AVL trees with this extra indexing information, offer a good balance, supporting all these operations in logarithmic time, which is efficient even for large datasets.

For static dictionaries, perfect hashing is a technique that creates a hash function with no collisions, so every key maps to a unique slot. This makes searching extremely fast, but building such a hash function can be complex. When you need to do more than just exact searches, like range queries or nearest neighbor searches, binary search trees are a better choice. You can even build an optimal binary search tree if you know the probability of searching for each key. This tree minimizes the average search time by arranging keys so that frequently searched keys are near the top.

Building an optimal binary search tree involves considering both successful searches (where the key is found) and unsuccessful searches (where the key isn’t in the dictionary). The tree’s cost depends on how deep you have to go to find or fail to find a key, weighted by the probability of each search. Finding the best tree can be done with dynamic programming, which breaks the problem into smaller parts and combines solutions, but it can be computationally expensive for large numbers of keys.

In dynamic dictionaries, the main operations are searching for a key, inserting a new key-element pair, and removing a key. Additional operations might include iterating over all keys in order, or accessing and removing elements by their rank or position. The efficiency of these operations depends on the data structure used. Balanced binary search trees provide good worst-case guarantees, keeping operations fast even as the dictionary grows.

Removing elements from a binary search tree depends on the node’s structure. If the node is a leaf, you can just remove it. If it has one child, you replace the node with its child. If it has two children, you replace it with either the largest node in its left subtree or the smallest node in its right subtree, which simplifies the removal to one of the first two cases. This process keeps the tree’s structure valid.

Balanced search trees are designed to keep their height small, usually proportional to the logarithm of the number of nodes. This ensures that operations like search, insert, and delete remain efficient. There are different types of balanced trees, such as AVL trees, red-black trees, and B-trees, each with its own rules for maintaining balance. These trees are widely used in databases and file systems because they handle large amounts of data efficiently.

Overall, dictionaries and indexed search trees are powerful tools for organizing and accessing data. Choosing the right data structure depends on the types of operations you need and the performance requirements of your application. Understanding how these structures work helps you make better decisions when designing software that manages data.

title: 9. AVL Trees
content:
Today, we’re going to talk about two important types of balanced binary search trees: AVL trees and red-black trees. These structures help us keep data organized so that searching, inserting, and deleting elements can be done efficiently, even as the data changes over time.

Let’s start with the problem these trees solve. When you store data in a binary search tree, the time it takes to find or update something depends on the tree’s height. If the tree becomes unbalanced, it can get very tall and skinny, making operations slow—almost like a linked list. Balanced trees keep the height small relative to the number of nodes, which keeps operations fast.

An AVL tree is one of the earliest balanced trees. It’s a binary search tree with a special rule: for every node, the difference in height between its left and right subtrees can only be -1, 0, or 1. This difference is called the balance factor. By enforcing this, AVL trees make sure the tree stays roughly balanced.

Because of this balance, the height of an AVL tree grows slowly as you add more nodes. It’s never more than about 1.44 times the logarithm of the number of nodes, which means operations like search, insert, and delete stay efficient.

When you insert a new node into an AVL tree, you first add it like in a normal binary search tree. Then, you walk back up the tree, updating balance factors. If you find a node where the balance factor becomes 2 or -2, the tree is unbalanced and needs fixing. This fixing is done through rotations, which are ways of rearranging the tree to restore balance.

There are four main types of imbalances depending on where the new node was added relative to the unbalanced node. These are called LL, RR, LR, and RL. LL and RR imbalances are fixed with a single rotation, while LR and RL require two rotations, called double rotations. After these rotations, the tree is balanced again, and the height of the affected subtree doesn’t increase.

Deletion in AVL trees is a bit more complicated. After removing a node, you again update balance factors going up the tree. If you find an imbalance, you perform rotations similar to those used in insertion. However, deletion can cause a chain of imbalances up the tree, so you might need multiple rotations. Still, the number of rotations is proportional to the height of the tree, which is logarithmic in the number of nodes.

Now, red-black trees offer a different approach to balancing. Instead of strictly limiting the height difference like AVL trees, red-black trees assign a color—red or black—to each node and enforce rules about how these colors can appear along paths from the root to the leaves. For example, the root and all leaves are black, no two red nodes can be adjacent, and every path from the root to a leaf has the same number of black nodes.

These color rules ensure the tree remains balanced enough to guarantee that its height is at most twice the logarithm of the number of nodes. This is a bit looser than AVL trees but still keeps operations efficient.

When inserting into a red-black tree, you add the new node as red. This might cause two red nodes in a row, which violates the rules. To fix this, you perform color flips and rotations, similar to AVL rotations but guided by the color rules. The process ensures the tree remains balanced without too many rotations.

Deletion in red-black trees is more involved because removing a black node can cause a “black deficiency” in a subtree, breaking the color balance. Fixing this involves a series of color changes and rotations, sometimes moving the problem up the tree until balance is restored.

In practice, red-black trees are often preferred because they require fewer rotations on average and are easier to implement efficiently. Many programming libraries use red-black trees to implement ordered maps and sets.

Both AVL and red-black trees guarantee that search, insert, and delete operations run in logarithmic time, which is crucial for performance in many applications. Understanding how they maintain balance through rotations and color rules helps you appreciate how data structures keep things running smoothly behind the scenes.

title: 10. B-Trees
content:
When dealing with very large collections of data, especially those stored on disk rather than in fast memory, the way we organize and search through that data becomes really important. Traditional binary search trees like AVL or Red-Black trees work well in memory because they keep the tree balanced and the height relatively low. But when these trees are stored on disk, each node access can mean a slow disk read, which adds up quickly. For example, if you have about a billion keys, an AVL tree might have a height around 40, meaning you could need up to 40 disk reads to find a key. Since each disk read can take a fraction of a second, this search could take several seconds, which is too slow for most applications.

To solve this problem, we use a different kind of tree called a B-tree. The main idea behind B-trees is to reduce the height of the tree by allowing each node to hold many keys and have many children. Instead of just two children like in a binary tree, a B-tree node might have dozens or even hundreds of children. This makes the tree much shorter, so fewer disk reads are needed to find or update a key.

A B-tree is a type of m-way search tree, where each node can have up to m children and m-1 keys. The tree is balanced, meaning all the leaves are at the same level, and it follows rules about how many children each node must have. The root must have at least two children if the tree isn’t empty, and every other internal node must have at least about half of the maximum number of children. This keeps the tree balanced and prevents it from becoming too skinny or too wide.

For example, a 2-3 tree is a B-tree where each node can have 2 or 3 children, and a 2-3-4 tree allows 2, 3, or 4 children per node. These are special cases of B-trees with small orders. When the order is larger, the nodes can hold more keys, which makes the tree even shorter.

The height of a B-tree grows very slowly compared to the number of keys it holds. Because each node covers a large range of keys, the tree doesn’t need to be very tall to hold billions of keys. This is why B-trees are so useful for databases and file systems where data is stored on disk.

When inserting a new key into a B-tree, you first find the correct leaf node where the key should go. If that node has space, you just add the key in the right order. But if the node is full, it splits into two nodes, and the middle key moves up to the parent node. This splitting can happen all the way up to the root, and if the root splits, the tree grows taller by one level.

Deletion is a bit more complicated because removing a key can cause a node to have too few keys. To fix this, the tree can borrow a key from a sibling node if that sibling has extra keys, or it can merge with a sibling and pull a key down from the parent. This process keeps the tree balanced and may reduce the height if the root ends up with only one child.

One important thing about B-trees is how they minimize disk accesses. Searching requires reading nodes from the root down to a leaf, so the number of disk reads equals the height of the tree. Insertions and deletions may cause extra writes due to splitting or merging nodes, but overall, the number of disk operations is kept low because the tree is short and wide.

There’s also a variant called the B+-tree, which is very common in databases. In a B+-tree, all the actual data is stored only in the leaf nodes, and the internal nodes only store keys to guide the search. The leaves are linked together in a list, which makes it easy to do range queries or scan through the data sequentially. This structure improves performance for many database operations.

In summary, B-trees and their variants are designed to handle very large datasets efficiently when stored on disk. They keep the tree balanced and shallow by allowing nodes to hold many keys, which reduces the number of slow disk accesses needed for searching, inserting, or deleting keys. This makes them a fundamental data structure for databases and file systems.

title: 11. Splay Trees
content:
Today, we’re going to talk about splay trees, a type of binary search tree that adjusts itself to improve efficiency over time. The main idea behind splay trees is that when you access a node—whether by searching, inserting, or deleting—it moves that node closer to the root. This way, nodes that are accessed frequently become easier and faster to reach in the future. While some operations might take longer in the worst case, the average time per operation over many operations tends to be quite efficient.

Splay trees support the usual operations you expect from binary search trees: searching for a key, inserting a new key, deleting a key, splitting the tree into two based on a key, and joining two trees together. What makes splay trees special is how they handle these operations with a process called splaying, which rearranges the tree to keep it balanced in a way that favors recently accessed nodes.

There are two main ways to implement splay trees: bottom-up and top-down. In the bottom-up approach, you first perform the operation like you would in a regular binary search tree. After that, you identify a particular node called the splay node, which depends on the operation you just did. For example, if you searched for a key and found it, that node becomes the splay node. If you didn’t find it, the splay node is the parent of the place where the search ended. Once you have the splay node, you perform a series of rotations to move it up to the root of the tree. These rotations happen step by step, sometimes moving the node up one level, sometimes two, until it reaches the root. This restructuring helps keep the tree balanced in a way that favors recently accessed nodes.

Inserting and deleting work similarly. After inserting a new node or deleting an existing one, you splay the relevant node to the root. Splitting the tree involves inserting a new key and then splaying it to the root, which naturally divides the tree into two parts: one with keys smaller than the new key and one with keys larger. Joining two trees is simpler and doesn’t require splaying; it can be done efficiently by attaching one tree as a subtree of the other.

The downside of bottom-up splay trees is that in the worst case, the tree can become very tall, making some operations take linear time. However, over many operations, the average time per operation remains logarithmic, which is quite efficient.

Top-down splay trees take a different approach. Instead of performing the splay after the operation, they do it while moving down the tree. As you search for the node, you split the tree into two smaller trees: one with all elements smaller than the node you’re looking for, and one with all elements larger. During this descent, you perform rotations whenever you encounter certain patterns, which helps keep the tree balanced as you go. Once you reach the node, you combine these smaller trees back together with the node, resulting in a balanced tree with the accessed node at the root. This method tends to be faster in practice because it avoids some of the overhead of the bottom-up approach.

Both methods aim to keep frequently accessed nodes near the root, improving access times for those nodes. The choice between bottom-up and top-down often depends on the specific use case and implementation preferences, but top-down splaying is generally considered faster.

Overall, splay trees are useful when you expect certain elements to be accessed repeatedly, as they adapt to usage patterns over time. They offer good average performance for a variety of operations and can outperform other data structures like heaps in some scenarios, especially when many operations are performed in sequence. Understanding how splay trees work, especially the splaying process and the difference between bottom-up and top-down approaches, gives you a powerful tool for managing dynamic sets of data efficiently.

title: 12. Digital Search Trees and Binary Tries
content:
Today, we’re going to talk about two important data structures that help us efficiently store and search for keys made up of binary strings: Digital Search Trees and Binary Tries. These structures are especially useful when the keys are sequences of bits, like IP addresses in computer networks. Instead of comparing whole keys at once, these trees look at the bits one by one, which is similar in spirit to how radix sort works, but applied to searching.

Let’s start with Digital Search Trees, or DSTs. Imagine you have keys that are fixed-length binary strings, say 4 bits each, like 0110 or 1011. A DST organizes these keys in a binary tree where the root holds one key, and the rest of the keys are split based on their first bit. If a key starts with 0, it goes to the left subtree; if it starts with 1, it goes to the right subtree. Then, in each subtree, the process repeats but looks at the next bit of the keys. This way, the tree branches according to the bits of the keys, guiding you down the path that matches the key you’re searching for or inserting.

For example, if you start with an empty DST and insert the key 0110, that key becomes the root. Next, if you insert 0010, since it starts with 0, it goes to the left subtree of the root. If you then insert 1001, it goes to the right subtree because it starts with 1. This splitting continues as you add more keys, always looking at the next bit to decide which way to go.

The main advantage of DSTs is that searching, inserting, or deleting a key takes time proportional to the number of bits in the key. So if your keys are 32 bits long, like IPv4 addresses, the operations take about 32 steps. This is straightforward but can get expensive if keys are very long, like 128-bit IPv6 addresses.

Now, Binary Tries are a related but slightly different structure designed to be more efficient, especially for fixed-length keys. In a Binary Trie, internal nodes don’t store any data themselves; they just have pointers to left and right children. The actual keys are stored only at the leaves, which hold the dictionary pairs. When you search for a key, you follow the path determined by the bits of the key, moving left or right depending on whether the bit is 0 or 1. Because the keys are stored only at the leaves, you only need to compare the key once at the end of the search, making the search operation very efficient.

This structure is neat because it guarantees at most one key comparison per search, which is better than DSTs where you might compare keys multiple times as you move down the tree. The trade-off is that the trie can be larger in size because it stores nodes for every bit position, but the speed gain in searching often makes it worthwhile.

Things get a bit more complicated when keys have variable lengths, meaning some keys might be shorter than others. In this case, the Binary Trie needs to handle keys that end at different depths in the tree. To do this, each node can have not only pointers to left and right children but also fields to store keys that terminate exactly at that node. These fields hold the key that ends at the root of the left or right subtree or the single key that would otherwise be stored there. If no key ends at that node, these fields are empty. This setup allows the trie to handle variable-length keys without losing the efficiency of bitwise navigation, still requiring at most one key comparison during search.

When it comes to operations like search, insert, and delete, both DSTs and Binary Tries follow the bit-by-bit path down the tree. Searching is straightforward: you follow the bits of the key until you find the node or leaf that should contain it. Inserting involves navigating the tree similarly and adding the key in the correct place. Deletion is a bit trickier, especially for variable-length keys, because you might need to update those special fields or restructure parts of the tree to maintain its properties.

Overall, Digital Search Trees and Binary Tries are useful when you’re dealing with keys that are naturally represented as bit strings, like IP addresses. DSTs are simpler but can be slower for long keys, while Binary Tries optimize search by reducing the number of key comparisons. Handling variable-length keys requires some extra care but can be done efficiently with the right structure. These data structures are foundational in areas like IP routing and packet filtering, where fast and reliable key lookup is essential.

title: 13. Compressed and Multibit Tries
content:
Let’s talk about tries, a type of data structure used to store keys like strings or sequences of bits. A basic binary trie branches on each bit of a key, going left or right depending on whether the bit is 0 or 1. But this can be inefficient because many nodes end up having only one child, which wastes space and slows down operations. To fix this, we use something called a compressed binary trie. In a compressed trie, we remove all nodes that have only one child. Instead of branching on every single bit, we skip over sequences of bits that don’t cause a branch. Each branch node keeps track of which bit to look at next, so even though we’re skipping bits, we know exactly where to check. This reduces the number of nodes and the height of the trie, making searches and updates faster.

Now, tries aren’t limited to just bits. When keys are made up of digits or characters, we can use higher order tries that branch on more than two options at each node. For example, if you have 9-digit numbers as keys, you can build a 10-way trie where each node branches on one digit from 0 to 9. This trie will have a height of at most 10, one level per digit. Searching in this trie means following the digits of the key down the tree. Compared to balanced binary trees like AVL or red-black trees, tries can be more efficient for this kind of data because they avoid repeated comparisons of whole keys and instead just follow the digits directly.

Sometimes keys have different lengths, which can cause problems if one key is a prefix of another. For example, if you have the key "0123" and also "012345", the trie might confuse the shorter key as just a prefix of the longer one. To handle this, we add a special end-of-key character to each key. This character marks where the key ends, so the trie knows that "0123" is a complete key and not just the start of a longer one. This simple addition removes ambiguity and keeps the trie structure clean.

Another way to optimize tries is by adding extra information to the edges or nodes. Each branch node can store a pointer to an element in its subtree, which helps when you skip over multiple bits or characters at once. This pointer lets you recover the skipped parts of the key during a search, so you don’t lose track of what you’re matching. This technique helps keep the trie’s height low and speeds up lookups.

Multibit tries take this idea further by allowing each node to branch on multiple bits at once, not just one. Instead of checking a single bit to decide which way to go, a node might look at, say, 3 or 8 bits together. This increases the branching factor and reduces the height of the trie. Multibit tries are especially useful in applications like Internet routing, where keys are IP addresses with variable-length prefixes. Routers need to find the longest matching prefix for a destination address quickly, and multibit tries help by cutting down the number of levels they have to check.

In routing, the router has a large table of rules that map destination prefixes to output ports. These rules can be ranges or prefix filters, and when multiple rules match a destination, the router uses tie breakers like the longest prefix match or highest priority to decide which rule to apply. Because routing tables can have millions of entries and IP addresses can be quite long, efficient data structures are essential to keep up with high-speed network traffic.

There are hardware solutions like TCAMs, which can match bits with wildcards very fast, but they have limitations in cost, power, and scalability, especially for newer, longer IPv6 addresses. Software solutions often rely on tries, including multibit tries, to balance speed and memory use. These tries can be compacted and optimized to handle large routing tables efficiently.

When it comes to complexity, a basic 1-bit trie takes time proportional to the length of the key for each operation. Fixed-stride tries use the same number of bits at each level, which can reduce the height but might increase memory use. Variable-stride tries allow different nodes to use different numbers of bits, offering more flexibility and better memory efficiency. Finding the best stride lengths to minimize memory while keeping the trie short is an optimization problem researchers study.

Finally, some applications require filtering on pairs of keys, like source and destination addresses in networking. Two-dimensional tries branch on both keys simultaneously, allowing complex filtering rules to be applied efficiently. These can be built as 1-bit or multibit tries, depending on the needs.

Overall, tries and their variants are powerful tools for storing and searching keys, especially when you need fast prefix matching or have large sets of keys with structured formats like IP addresses or phone numbers. By compressing tries, using multibit branching, and adding clever optimizations, we can build data structures that handle millions of entries quickly and efficiently.

title: 14. Suffix Trees
content:
Let’s talk about suffix trees, a data structure that helps us work with strings in a very efficient way. To start, it’s important to understand what we mean by strings, substrings, and subsequences. A string is just a sequence of characters, like the word “cater.” A substring is a part of that string made up of consecutive characters, so “ate” is a substring of “cater” because those letters appear together in order. But “car” is not a substring because those letters don’t appear consecutively. A subsequence is a bit more flexible—it’s a sequence of characters that appear in the same order but not necessarily next to each other. So in “cater,” both “ate” and “car” are subsequences, even though “car” isn’t a substring.

One common problem with strings is pattern matching: given a big string, can we quickly find out if a smaller string appears inside it? For example, if you have a long DNA sequence, you might want to know if a particular gene sequence is part of it. Traditional methods like the Knuth-Morris-Pratt algorithm preprocess the smaller string you’re searching for, which works well for one or a few queries but can get slow if you have many queries. Suffix trees take a different approach by preprocessing the big string itself, which makes answering many queries much faster.

So what exactly is a suffix tree? Imagine you take every suffix of a string—that is, every ending part of the string starting from each character—and organize them in a tree structure. For example, if your string is “sleeper,” the suffixes are “sleeper,” “leeper,” “eeper,” “eper,” “per,” “er,” and “r.” A suffix tree is a compressed trie that stores all these suffixes in a way that common parts are shared, so it doesn’t waste space repeating the same sequences. This structure lets you quickly check if a substring exists by seeing if it matches the start of any suffix.

There’s a small complication when the last character of the string appears multiple times. Some suffixes might then be prefixes of others, which can confuse the tree structure. To fix this, we add a special character at the end of the string that doesn’t appear anywhere else, like a “#.” This makes every suffix unique and avoids overlap problems.

Building a suffix tree involves creating a compressed trie of all suffixes. While a straightforward method might take more time, there are efficient algorithms that can build the tree in time proportional to the length of the string, which is pretty fast. Once built, you can search for any substring by following edges in the tree that match the substring’s characters. If you reach a leaf node, the substring appears exactly once. If you end up at an internal node, it means the substring appears multiple times.

If you want to find all occurrences of a substring, the suffix tree can be augmented by linking all the leaf nodes in order and having internal nodes keep track of the range of leaves in their subtree. This way, you can quickly list all positions where the substring appears without extra searching.

Suffix trees also help find the longest repeating substring in a string—that is, the longest piece that appears more than once. By labeling internal nodes with how many suffixes they represent, you can find the node that corresponds to the longest substring repeated at least a certain number of times.

Another interesting use is finding the longest common substring between two strings. For example, if you have “carport” and “airports,” the longest common substring is “rport.” To find this efficiently, you combine the two strings with unique end markers and build a suffix tree for the combined string. Then, by looking for the deepest node that has suffixes from both original strings, you can identify the longest shared substring quickly.

In summary, suffix trees are a powerful way to organize all suffixes of a string so that substring queries and related problems can be solved efficiently. They’re especially useful when you have a large string and many queries or when you want to find repeating patterns or common parts between strings. The key idea is that by preprocessing the big string into this tree structure, you can answer questions about substrings much faster than by checking each query individually.
